title: Retrieval Quality
scopeHtml: Scope: Hybrid search, reranking, query rewriting, HyDE, filters, multi-hop and graph approaches.

notes.title: Hybrid search
notes.html:
Why dense retrieval alone is not enough. Embeddings capture meaning but blur exact tokens: product codes ("XJ-4471"), error messages, names, acronyms, version numbers, rare technical terms, negations and numbers. Keyword search (BM25) is the opposite: precise on exact terms, blind to paraphrase and synonyms.

BM25 in short. A probabilistic ranking function over an inverted index: score(term) = IDF(term) × (tf × (k1+1)) / (tf + k1 × (1 − b + b × doclen/avglen)). Rewards rare query terms (IDF), saturates term frequency, normalizes by document length. Fast, explainable, no training.

Hybrid search runs both retrievers in parallel and fuses their ranked lists.

Fusion methods.

  • Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF): score(d) = Σ 1 / (k + rank_i(d)) with k ≈ 60 across the lists. No score normalization needed; robust default.
  • Weighted score fusion: normalize scores (min-max or z-score) and combine α·dense + (1−α)·sparse; tune α on your eval.
  • Learned sparse retrievers (SPLADE) and multi-vector (ColBERT) are further options bridging both worlds.

Tuning. Evaluate dense-only, BM25-only, and hybrid on a labelled set with recall@k/nDCG; hybrid is usually best on enterprise/technical corpora. Query analysis can route: identifier-looking queries lean lexical; natural-language questions lean semantic.

Implementation notes. Many stores support hybrid natively (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Weaviate, Qdrant, Vespa, Postgres full-text + pgvector). Use language-appropriate analyzers (stemming, stopwords, tokenization for CJK), field boosts (title > body), and phrase/boolean filters.

Real life. Searching a shop by description ("red running shoes") and by SKU ("RX-4471"); you want both to work.

notes.title: Reranking
notes.html:
Two-stage retrieval. Stage 1 (fast, recall-oriented): bi-encoder and/or BM25 retrieve 50 to 200 candidates. Stage 2 (slow, precision-oriented): a cross-encoder reranker reads each (query, candidate) pair together and outputs a relevance score; keep the top 3 to 10 for the prompt.

Why it helps. Query and passage attend to each other, capturing negation, conditions, exact constraints and answerability that vector similarity misses. Typical gains: +5 to 20 points of precision@k or nDCG; also improves context quality, reducing prompt tokens.

Options. Open cross-encoders (bge-reranker, MiniLM-based), hosted reranker APIs (Cohere Rerank, Voyage), late-interaction models (ColBERT), or LLM-based reranking (listwise/pointwise prompts; powerful but costly and slower).

Costs and controls. Latency scales with candidates × length: 100 candidates × 512 tokens can be 100 to 400 ms on a GPU. Mitigate: cap candidates, truncate passages, batch on GPU, cache scores for repeated queries, use smaller rerankers, apply rerank only when needed (e.g. low first-stage confidence).

Thresholding. Reranker scores are better calibrated than raw cosine: use a threshold (or a gap between top scores) to decide "not enough evidence" and let the model answer "I don't know" or ask a clarifying question.

Evaluation. Measure with and without reranking on recall@k, nDCG@k, and end-answer quality; check latency budget impact.

Real life. Shortlisting CVs by headline, then interviewing the shortlist.

notes.title: Query transformation
notes.html:
The problem. User questions are poor search queries: elliptical in multi-turn chat ("and for Europe?"), multi-part, vague, using different vocabulary than the documents.

Techniques.

  • Conversational rewriting: an LLM turns the latest message plus history into a standalone query.
  • Query expansion: add synonyms/related terms (for BM25) or generate multiple paraphrases (multi-query) and merge results (RRF).
  • Decomposition: split a complex question into sub-questions, retrieve for each, then synthesize (sequential for dependent ones).
  • HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings): have the model write a hypothetical answer, embed that, and retrieve real passages similar to it; bridges the query-document style gap, but can inject model hallucinations into the search.
  • Step-back prompting: ask a more general question to retrieve background principles.
  • Intent classification/routing: decide which index, tool, or strategy fits (FAQ vs docs vs database).
  • Metadata extraction: parse filters from the query ("invoices from March 2025 for Acme") and apply them as structured filters (self-querying retriever).
  • Spelling/acronym normalization using a glossary.

Trade-offs. Each LLM-based transform adds latency (200 ms to 2 s) and cost, and can introduce drift from the user's intent. Use selectively, measure the gain on the eval, and fall back to the raw query if transformation fails.

Real life. A librarian who asks a clarifying question or rephrases your request before searching the stacks.

notes.title: Metadata filtering and access control
notes.html:
Filters improve relevance and efficiency. Restrict by document type, product, version, language, date range, region, tenant, or source system before or during vector search.

Access control (security-critical).

  • Store ACL metadata (user, group, role, tenant ids) with each chunk; sync permission changes from the source system.
  • Enforce at query time inside the retrieval layer by applying the requesting user's identity as a filter. Never retrieve everything and rely on the LLM to withhold restricted text.
  • Prefer separate indexes/namespaces per tenant for strong isolation, or filtered single indexes with tested guarantees.
  • Consider document-level and chunk-level permissions; handle revocation delays and cached results.
  • Log which documents were used for each answer (audit).
  • Test with canary documents: a user without access must never see them in results, citations, or error messages.

Technical pitfalls. Post-filtering ANN results can return fewer than k (or zero) when filters are selective; use index-native filtering and evaluate recall under realistic filters. Filter cardinality, index design (partitioning by tenant), and filter-aware ANN parameters matter at scale.

Freshness filters/boosts. Boost recent documents, exclude superseded versions, or filter on status = "published".

Real life. A records office that only fetches the files your badge allows.

notes.title: Multi-hop and graph approaches
notes.html:
Multi-hop questions need several pieces of evidence connected by reasoning: "Which team owns the service that caused last week's outage, and who is its on-call?" Single-shot retrieval seldom finds all pieces.

Approaches.

  • Iterative / agentic retrieval: the model retrieves, reasons about what's missing, issues a new query, repeats until sufficient or a step limit. Flexible; costlier and less predictable; log each step.
  • Decomposition + sequential retrieval (see query transformation).
  • Knowledge graphs / GraphRAG: extract entities and relations from the corpus into a graph; retrieve by traversing relationships and community summaries; strong for corpus-wide "global" questions ("What are the main themes?") and relationship queries; expensive to build and keep fresh; extraction errors propagate.
  • Hierarchical retrieval / RAPTOR: build a tree of summaries; retrieve at the right level of abstraction.
  • Text-to-SQL / API tools for structured data joins.

When to adopt. Only when evaluation shows single-hop hybrid + rerank failing on a significant class of real questions. Complexity must pay for itself.

Real life. Following footnotes from one paper to the next until you find the original source.

notes.title: Chunking strategies beyond fixed size
notes.html:
Semantic chunking. Embed sentences, split where similarity between adjacent sentences/windows falls below a threshold or where topic shifts; yields coherent chunks of variable length. Costs extra embedding compute and tuning.

Parent-document retrieval. Index small chunks (precise matching) but return their larger parent section (rich context). Reduces fragmentation without diluting embeddings.

Sentence-window retrieval. Match single sentences, return window of ±N sentences.

Contextual retrieval. Prepend LLM-generated context to each chunk ("This chunk is from the 2024 refund policy, section on opened items…") before embedding and BM25 indexing; reported to cut retrieval failures substantially at modest preprocessing cost (prompt caching makes it cheap).

Proposition/atomic-fact chunking. Rewrite text into self-contained statements; high precision, more chunks.

Late chunking / long-context embedding models. Embed the whole document with a long-context model, then pool token embeddings per chunk, preserving cross-chunk context.

Multi-representation indexing. Index summaries, hypothetical questions, or keywords that point to the original chunk.

Evaluate chunking like any hyperparameter: sweep sizes/strategies against your labelled retrieval set; there is no universal best.

Real life. Finding the paragraph, then reading the whole page around it.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Hybrid search. Dense retrieval handles meaning, BM25 handles exact terms; fuse with RRF (k≈60) or tuned weights; hybrid is the strong default for technical and enterprise content.

Reranking. Retrieve 50 to 200, rerank with a cross-encoder to the top 3 to 10: bigger precision, better prompts, calibrated thresholds; budget the latency (100 to 400 ms) and cap candidates.

Query transformation. Rewrite using history, expand/multi-query, decompose, HyDE, step-back, route by intent, extract metadata filters. Each adds latency and risk; adopt based on eval gains.

Filtering and security. Use metadata filters and enforce permissions in the retrieval layer; test isolation with canaries; avoid post-filter recall collapse by using index-native filtering.

Multi-hop. Iterative/agentic retrieval, decomposition, GraphRAG/hierarchical summaries for relational or corpus-wide questions — use only when single-hop fails measurably.

Chunking upgrades. Semantic, parent-document, sentence-window, contextual (LLM-added context), propositions, late chunking, multi-representation; tune empirically.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Dense for meaning, sparse for exact terms, fuse with RRF."
  • "Retrieve wide, rerank narrow."
  • "Enforce ACLs in the retriever, never in the prompt."
  • "Add multi-hop machinery only after the eval shows single-hop is the bottleneck."
